records.title: Statement on Inclusive and Sustainable Artificial Intelligence for People and the Planet
records.original_title: Déclaration sur une intelligence artificielle inclusive et durable pour les peuples et la planète
records.issuing_body: Signatories of the AI Action Summit, Paris (hosted by the French Presidency): 63 countries, the African Union Commission and the EU
records.summary: This summit outcome moves the emphasis from frontier safety to inclusion, sustainability, openness and the future of work. It still calls for AI that is 'human rights based, human-centric, ethical, safe, secure and trustworthy', credits the Bletchley and Seoul safety work, and commits to address AI risks to information integrity. It also backs a UN Global Dialogue on AI governance and an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
records.notes: Issued after the AI Action Summit, 10-11 Feb 2025. The United States and United Kingdom did not sign. The signatory list on the Élysée page shows 65 signatories (63 countries plus the AU Commission and the EU). The International AI Safety Report 2025 was published for this summit.

records.title: New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact
records.issuing_body: Participants of the India AI Impact Summit 2026, New Delhi (hosted by the Government of India)
records.summary: This outcome of the fourth summit in the series is built on three 'Sutras' (People, Planet, Progress) and seven pillars, including 'secure and trusted AI'. That pillar treats security of AI systems as foundational to trust, says understanding of potential security risks needs to deepen, and notes voluntary industry measures and policy frameworks across the AI lifecycle. All deliverables are voluntary and non-binding, including a Trusted AI Commons platform for safety tools, benchmarks and best practices.
records.notes: The summit's high-level segment was held in New Delhi in Feb 2026; PIB gives 18-19 Feb, while All India Radio reported on 21 Feb that it 'concluded yesterday'. The exact adoption day is unclear, so only the month is given. PIB's endorsement list, current to 5 Mar 2026, shows 92 countries and international organisations, including the USA, China and the EU; earlier reports said 88. Companion outcome documents include the Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI, the Framework for the Trusted AI Commons, a Guidance Note on AI Governance, 'AI and Child Safety', and the Guiding Principles on Resilient, Innovative and Efficient AI. The New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments (19 Feb 2026) are voluntary company commitments on sharing anonymised AI-usage insights and on multilingual and contextual evaluations; they contain no explicit safety-testing commitments.

records.title: The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit, 1-2 November 2023
records.issuing_body: Governments attending the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park (28 countries and the EU), hosted by the UK Government
records.summary: First intergovernmental declaration focused on 'frontier AI' (highly capable general-purpose models). It warns of serious, even catastrophic, harm from misuse and loss of control, singles out cybersecurity, biotechnology and disinformation risks, and calls for shared scientific understanding, risk-based policies, safety testing and evaluation, and transparency from frontier developers.
records.notes: Signed at the first AI Safety Summit, 1-2 Nov 2023. Signatories include the US, China and the EU. It launched the summit series: Seoul (May 2024), Paris (Feb 2025), New Delhi (Feb 2026). It also led to the International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI. GOV.UK shows the page as last updated 13 Feb 2025; the text itself is unchanged.

verification.note: GOV.UK page fetched. Title confirmed; first published 1 Nov 2023, last updated 13 Feb 2025. Frontier-risk content confirmed. The signatory count (28 + EU) comes from the researcher's background knowledge and was not re-read on the page.

records.title: Seoul Declaration for safe, innovative and inclusive AI by participants attending the Leaders' Session: AI Seoul Summit, 21 May 2024
records.issuing_body: Leaders of Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Republic of Korea, Singapore, UK, US and the EU (AI Seoul Summit, co-hosted by the Republic of Korea and the UK)
records.summary: Leaders treat AI safety, innovation and inclusivity as linked goals. They endorse risk-based governance across the AI lifecycle and back the creation or expansion of AI safety institutes and networks between them. They also point to the Hiroshima Code of Conduct and the Frontier AI Safety Commitments as ways to put interoperable governance into practice.
records.notes: Adopted at the virtual Leaders' Session on 21 May 2024. The Seoul Statement of Intent toward International Cooperation on AI Safety Science is annexed to it. It anticipated the AI Action Summit in France.

verification.note: GOV.UK publication page and HTML text fetched. Title, 21 May 2024 date and the 10 countries + EU signatory list confirmed.

records.title: Seoul Statement of Intent toward International Cooperation on AI Safety Science, AI Seoul Summit 2024 (Annex)
records.short_title: Seoul Statement of Intent on AI Safety Science
records.issuing_body: Leaders of Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Republic of Korea, Singapore, UK, US and the EU
records.summary: Signatories commit to work together on AI safety science through publicly backed bodies such as AI Safety Institutes. Planned work includes aligning technical methods, sharing information on model capabilities, limitations and risks, monitoring harms and safety incidents, and exchanging evaluations and datasets. They also state a shared aim to build an international network to speed up AI safety science.
records.notes: Annex to the Seoul Declaration. It led to the International Network of AI Safety Institutes, launched in Nov 2024 and renamed in Dec 2025.

records.title: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024
records.issuing_body: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (published for the AI Seoul Summit co-hosts); commitments made by 20 AI organisations
records.summary: Leading AI developers commit to assess frontier-model risks across the lifecycle and to set and monitor thresholds for intolerable severe risks. They agree not to develop or deploy a model if those risks cannot be kept below the thresholds, and to maintain internal accountability. They also commit to publish a safety framework and report publicly on implementation, with deeper information shared with trusted actors such as home governments.
records.notes: The original 16 signatories were Amazon, Anthropic, Cohere, Google, G42, IBM, Inflection AI, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral AI, Naver, OpenAI, Samsung Electronics, Technology Innovation Institute, xAI and Zhipu.ai. Magic, Minimax, 01.ai and NVIDIA were added on 7 Feb 2025, making 20. Signatories committed to publish safety frameworks before the Paris AI Action Summit (Feb 2025). These are company commitments, included because governments published and brokered them.

verification.note: GOV.UK page fetched: published 21 May 2024, last updated 7 Feb 2025. HTML text fetched; 20 signatories and the three outcomes confirmed.

records.title: Seoul Ministerial Statement for advancing AI safety, innovation and inclusivity: AI Seoul Summit 2024
records.issuing_body: Ministers of 27 countries and a representative of the EU (AI Seoul Summit ministerial session)
records.summary: Ministers commit to frameworks for managing frontier-model risks, including credible external evaluation, and to work with stakeholders on thresholds at which unmitigated risks would be severe. Named examples are models that meaningfully help non-state actors acquire chemical or biological weapons, and models that evade human oversight through deception or autonomous replication. They ask AI safety institutes to share evaluation practices and datasets.
records.notes: Signatories include the US, UK, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Türkiye, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda and the EU. China is not on the list. Ministers planned to bring threshold proposals to the AI Action Summit in France.

records.title: Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy
records.issuing_body: African Union Executive Council (45th Ordinary Session, Accra); African Union Commission
records.summary: A development-focused continental AI strategy with a focus area on minimising risks. It names bias, privacy, disinformation and election manipulation, surveillance, deepfakes, cyber threats and military uses, and calls for technical standards on AI safety and security. It recommends agile, risk-based regulation, impact assessments, transparency registers, red-teaming, national and regional AI councils, and an annual AI safety and security conference.
records.notes: Endorsed by the AU Executive Council at its 45th Ordinary Session, Accra, 18-19 Jul 2024. Published on au.int on 9 Aug 2024. It has six focus areas, one of them an inclusive governance and regulatory framework.

verification.note: au.int document page fetched: title, endorsement 18-19 Jul 2024 and 9 Aug 2024 page date confirmed. Strategy PDF fetched: focus areas and the risk and safety provisions confirmed.

records.title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law
records.issuing_body: Council of Europe Committee of Ministers
records.summary: The first legally binding international treaty on AI. Parties must ensure that activities across the AI lifecycle are consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law, through risk and impact assessment, transparency, oversight, accountability and remedies. It applies fully to the public sector; for the private sector, Parties choose how to address risks.
records.notes: Adopted by the Committee of Ministers on 17 May 2024 and opened for signature in Vilnius on 5 Sep 2024. It enters into force on the first day of the month after a three-month period starting from the fifth ratification, of which at least three must be CoE member states. The CoE page lists 21 signatories: Albania, Andorra, Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Norway, Republic of Moldova, San Marino, Switzerland, Ukraine, UK, Canada, EU, Israel, Japan, USA and Uruguay. The EU ratified on 15 May 2026 at the 135th Committee of Ministers session in Chișinău. As of Oct 2026 the CoE AI page lists only the EU as a Party and no entry into force has been announced. A June 2026 CDNET report urges ratification 'with a view to achieving early entry into force'. The Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies (CDNET), which replaced the CAI, is the treaty's custodian; first plenary 15-17 Apr 2026, second plenary 21-23 Oct 2026.

records.title: Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems
records.issuing_body: G7 Leaders (Hiroshima AI Process, Japanese G7 Presidency)
records.summary: Eleven risk-based principles for organisations developing advanced AI systems, including foundation models and generative AI. They cover pre- and post-deployment risk identification and mitigation, transparency reporting, information sharing, governance and risk policies, security controls, content provenance, safety research and international standards. The principles build on the OECD AI Principles and are a living document meant to apply while governments develop regulation.
records.notes: Issued with the G7 Leaders' Statement on the Hiroshima AI Process (30 Oct 2023). Extended in Dec 2023 by the 'Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for All AI Actors' within the Comprehensive Policy Framework.

records.title: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems
records.issuing_body: G7 Leaders (Hiroshima AI Process, Japanese G7 Presidency)
records.summary: Voluntary guidance that turns the Guiding Principles into 11 actions for advanced-AI developers. They include red-teaming and testing before and after deployment, mitigating risks such as weapons misuse and cyber threats, post-deployment monitoring and incident sharing, and public transparency reports. Other actions cover governance and risk policies, security of model weights, content authentication such as watermarking, safety research, international standards and data protection.
records.notes: The OECD's Hiroshima AI Process (HAIP) Reporting Framework, launched 7 Feb 2025, monitors how companies apply the Code. The Seoul Declaration (May 2024) treats the Code as a focus for operationalising interoperable governance.

verification.note: MOFA English PDF fetched: title and the 11 actions confirmed. Date (30 Oct 2023) confirmed on the MOFA document page.

records.title: Hiroshima AI Process Comprehensive Policy Framework (Hiroshima AI Process G7 Digital & Tech Ministers' Statement)
records.issuing_body: G7 Digital and Tech Ministers; endorsed by G7 Leaders (6 Dec 2023)
records.summary: The G7's first international framework for governing advanced and generative AI, with four elements. These are the OECD report towards a G7 common understanding of generative AI, the Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles (extended to all AI actors), the International Code of Conduct for developers of advanced AI, and project-based cooperation on topics such as content authentication and disinformation.
records.notes: Agreed by G7 Digital & Tech Ministers on 1 Dec 2023 and endorsed by G7 Leaders on 6 Dec 2023. It includes the 'Hiroshima AI Process International Guiding Principles for All AI Actors'. Italy (2024) and Canada (2025) took the HAIP forward, and a HAIP Friends Group of non-G7 supporters now exists; it published a 'Friends Group Action Plan 2026'.

records.issuing_body: G7 Digital and Technology Ministers (French G7 Presidency)

records.title: International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI: interim report
records.jurisdiction: International AI Safety Report (AI Safety Summit process)
records.issuing_body: Independent expert group chaired by Yoshua Bengio; published by UK DSIT, the AI Safety (now Security) Institute and the Cabinet Office
records.summary: A science-based overview of general-purpose AI capabilities and risks. It covers malicious use, malfunctions (including disputed loss-of-control risk) and systemic risks such as labour-market disruption, and finds that mitigations such as benchmarking, red-teaming and auditing all have limits. It was commissioned under the Bletchley Declaration.
records.notes: Published for the AI Seoul Summit. Superseded by the full International AI Safety Report 2025 (29 Jan 2025). The GOV.UK page was updated on 22 Oct 2025 to link to the report's external website.

verification.note: GOV.UK page fetched: title, published 17 May 2024 and last updated 22 Oct 2025 confirmed.

records.title: International AI Safety Report 2025
records.jurisdiction: International AI Safety Report (AI Safety Summit process)
records.issuing_body: Independent expert panel chaired by Yoshua Bengio; secretariat in the UK AI Security Institute; published by UK DSIT
records.summary: The first full international scientific assessment of general-purpose AI capabilities and risks, written by about 100 experts. It covers malicious use, malfunctions and systemic risks, the rise of autonomous AI agents, and the state of risk-management techniques. It identifies key open research questions for policymakers, without making policy recommendations.
records.notes: Published for the Paris AI Action Summit. Two interim 'Key Updates' followed: 'First Key Update: Capabilities and Risk Implications' (15 Oct 2025) and 'Second Key Update: Technical Safeguards and Risk Management' (25 Nov 2025). Succeeded by the International AI Safety Report 2026 (3 Feb 2026). The old GOV.UK publication URL now redirects to internationalaisafetyreport.org, the report's official site, run with the UK AISI secretariat.

records.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
records.jurisdiction: International AI Safety Report (AI Safety Summit process)
records.issuing_body: Independent expert panel chaired by Yoshua Bengio; secretariat UK AI Security Institute and Mila; published under UK DSIT
records.summary: The second edition, written by over 100 experts, focuses on emerging risks at the frontier: malicious use (cyber, biological/chemical, manipulation), malfunctions including loss of control, and systemic risks. It highlights an 'evaluation gap': pre-deployment tests may not reflect real-world behaviour, and models increasingly detect when they are being tested. It describes layered safeguards and voluntary frontier safety frameworks as the main risk-management tools, with some jurisdictions starting to make them mandatory.
records.notes: Published 3 Feb 2026, before the India AI Impact Summit. An Extended Summary for Policymakers was published alongside it. Bengio also co-chairs the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, whose preliminary report followed on 1 Jul 2026.

verification.note: internationalaisafetyreport.org publication page fetched: title, 3 Feb 2026, chair, secretariat (UK AISI and Mila), DSIT 2026/001 and key findings confirmed. The PDF secondary URL was taken from search results and not fetched.

records.title: International Network of AI Safety Institutes – Joint Mission Statement (renamed International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science)
records.short_title: International Network of AI Safety Institutes
records.jurisdiction: International Network of AI Safety Institutes
records.issuing_body: Network members; launched by the US Department of Commerce and US Department of State at the inaugural convening in San Francisco
records.summary: All 10 founding members agreed a joint mission statement. It sets the Network up as a forum to build a common technical understanding of AI safety risks and mitigations, to support interoperable principles and best practices, and to encourage a shared global approach to AI safety. Its work centres on the science of AI testing and evaluation.
records.notes: Launched 20 Nov 2024 in San Francisco with the US as inaugural chair. Renamed 'International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science', confirmed at the Network's meeting in San Diego alongside NeurIPS; the UK announced this on 9 Dec 2025 and took on a 'Network Coordinator' role. The US now takes part through NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), the renamed US AI Safety Institute. On 13 Feb 2026 NIST published the Network's consensus practices and open questions on automated AI evaluations. The G7 Digital & Technology Ministerial Declaration (May 2026) tasks France with working with the Network and the OECD on comparable risk-assessment frameworks.

records.title: Summary of NATO's revised Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategy
records.issuing_body: NATO (agreed by Allies)
records.summary: Updates NATO's 2021 AI strategy for generative AI. It aims to lead by example in responsible use under six Principles of Responsible Use (lawfulness, accountability, explainability and traceability, reliability, governability, bias mitigation), and to build testing, evaluation, verification and validation capacity for safe use. It also addresses protection against adversarial AI and AI-enabled disinformation.
records.notes: Public summary published 10 Jul 2024; the full strategy is not public. It supersedes the summary of NATO's first AI Strategy (Oct 2021) while keeping its Principles of Responsible Use. The region is given as Europe, although NATO also includes the US and Canada.

records.title: Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence
records.issuing_body: OECD Council (at Ministerial level)
records.summary: The first intergovernmental standard on AI: five values-based principles and five recommendations to governments. Principle 1.4 (robustness, security and safety) requires AI to be safe throughout its lifecycle under normal use and foreseeable misuse. Where appropriate, there should be mechanisms to override, repair or safely decommission systems that risk undue harm, and to protect information integrity.
records.notes: Adopted 22 May 2019. On 8 Nov 2023 the definition of 'AI system' was revised. A further revision on 3 May 2024 at Ministerial level addressed generative AI, safety (override and decommissioning mechanisms) and information integrity. OECD.AI lists 47 adherents. The G20 AI Principles (2019) were drawn from it. OECD Recommendations are not legally binding but carry political commitment.

records.title: Political Declaration on Responsible Military Use of Artificial Intelligence and Autonomy
records.jurisdiction: Political Declaration on Responsible Military Use of AI (US-led initiative)
records.issuing_body: Endorsing states (initiative of the United States Department of State)
records.summary: Endorsing states commit to develop and use military AI, including autonomous systems, in line with international humanitarian law and within a responsible human chain of command. Ten measures cover legal reviews, senior-level oversight of high-consequence applications, minimising unintended bias, auditability, operator training against over-reliance, explicit intended uses, safety testing and assurance across the lifecycle, and safeguards to disengage or deactivate systems that behave unexpectedly.
records.notes: First launched at the REAIM Summit in The Hague on 16 Feb 2023. The revised text was released in Nov 2023, and the State Department announced 47 endorsing states on 13 Nov 2023 (per a DoD news article of 22 Nov 2023). records.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
records.issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
records.summary: The world's first comprehensive horizontal AI law. It takes a risk-based approach: it bans certain AI practices, sets requirements and conformity assessment for high-risk AI systems, imposes transparency duties (chatbots, deepfakes, machine-readable marking of AI-generated content), and sets obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, with extra duties for models with systemic risk. Enforcement is shared between the Commission's AI Office and national authorities.
records.notes: Adopted 13 June 2024. Published in OJ L on 12 July 2024. Entered into force 1 August 2024. Original phased application (Arts 111 and 113): 2 Feb 2025 for Chapters I–II (definitions, AI literacy, Art. 5 prohibitions 1–8); 2 Aug 2025 for GPAI model obligations (Ch. V), governance (AI Office, AI Board), notified bodies and penalties (except Art. 101 GPAI fines); 2 Aug 2026 for general application, including Art. 50 transparency, GPAI fines and the start of enforcement by the AI Office and national authorities; 2 Aug 2027 for Art. 6(1)/Annex I high-risk systems and for GPAI models placed on the market before 2 Aug 2025; 31 Dec 2030 for Annex X large-scale IT systems. AMENDED by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), in force 27 July 2026: Annex III (stand-alone) high-risk obligations moved from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 Dec 2027; Annex I (product-embedded) high-risk obligations moved from 2 Aug 2027 to 2 Aug 2028; a new Art. 5 prohibition (AI systems generating non-consensual sexual/intimate content or CSAM) applies from 2 Dec 2026; the Art. 50(2) marking grace period for generative systems already on the market ends 2 Dec 2026; the deadline for national regulatory sandboxes is 2 Aug 2027; the Art. 4 AI-literacy duty is simplified. EUR-Lex holds a consolidated version dated 27 July 2026 (CELEX 02024R1689-20260727). Commission report COM(2026) 234 (20 May 2026) found no immediate need to amend the Art. 5 or Annex III lists. On 9 Oct 2026 the Scientific Panel met in a special session on frontier AI safety risks, including recent loss-of-control incidents.

records.language: English (notice also in other EU languages)
records.summary: Template required under AI Act Art. 53(1)(d) that sets a 'common minimal baseline' for the public summary of content used to train a GPAI model. It supports transparency and the exercise of copyright and other rights.
records.notes: Published 24 July 2025. Using the template is mandatory in the sense that Art. 53(1)(d) requires the summary to follow the AI Office template. Last updated 26 March 2026.

verification.note: The Commission library page confirmed the title, publication date of 24 July 2025 and last update of 26 March 2026.

records.title: Draft guidance and reporting template on serious AI incidents (Article 73 AI Act)
records.issuing_body: European Commission (AI Office)
records.summary: Draft Commission guidance and a template for high-risk AI providers' duty under Art. 73 to report serious incidents to national market-surveillance authorities. It clarifies definitions, gives examples, explains the interplay with other reporting regimes, and aligns with the OECD AI Incidents Monitor and Common Reporting Framework.
records.notes: Draft published for consultation on 26 Sept 2025; the consultation closed 7 Nov 2025. Art. 73(7) required the guidance by 2 Aug 2025. A final version of the high-risk guidance was not found as of 11 Oct 2026; a Commission page lists a 'Template for reporting serious incidents by providers of high-risk AI systems' as published, but without a date. Separately, a final reporting template for serious incidents involving GPAI models with systemic risk (Art. 55; GPAI Code Commitment 9) was published on 4 Nov 2025. Art. 73 obligations follow the high-risk application dates, as revised by the Digital Omnibus.

verification.note: The Commission consultation page confirmed the draft status, publication on 26 Sept 2025 and the 7 Nov 2025 deadline. The Commission library page confirmed the GPAI serious-incident template of 4 Nov 2025. Final high-risk guidance could not be confirmed (web search budget was exhausted before a final check).

records.title: Draft Commission guidelines on the classification of high-risk AI systems
records.issuing_body: European Commission (AI Office)
records.summary: Draft guidelines under AI Act Art. 6(5) on classifying AI systems as high-risk, both as safety components of Annex I products and as Annex III use cases. They cover the Art. 6(3) filter for systems that do not pose a significant risk, with practical examples. The draft was published for targeted stakeholder consultation.
records.notes: The AI Act required these guidelines by 2 Feb 2026, but they were delayed. A draft was published on 19 May 2026 for targeted consultation, and the page was last updated 23 July 2026. No final version was found as of 11 Oct 2026. Their urgency eased after the Digital Omnibus moved Annex III obligations to 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I obligations to 2 Aug 2028.

verification.note: The Commission library page confirmed the title, draft status, publication date of 19 May 2026 and last update of 23 July 2026. COM(2026) 234 (20 May 2026) confirmed the guidelines were still in preparation. No final version was found.

records.title: Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council on the need to review the list of prohibited AI practices and of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III
records.issuing_body: European Commission
records.summary: The first annual assessment required by AI Act Art. 112(1). It concludes there is no immediate need to amend the Art. 5 prohibitions or the Annex III high-risk list because implementation experience is limited. It flags AI-generated child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate deepfakes as a possible regulatory gap to monitor.
records.notes: Adopted 20 May 2026. The gap it identified (CSAM and non-consensual intimate deepfakes) was addressed in parallel by the new Art. 5 prohibition in the Digital Omnibus on AI (agreed 7 May 2026; applies from 2 Dec 2026). The report also notes that national competent authorities were still being designated and that high-risk classification guidelines were still in preparation.

verification.note: The EUR-Lex HTML of COM(2026) 234 final loaded and confirmed the title, date (Brussels, 20 May 2026), Art. 112(1) basis and conclusions.

records.title: Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content
records.short_title: Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content
records.issuing_body: European Commission (AI Office), drafted by independent chairs; assessed as adequate by the Commission and the AI Board
records.summary: A voluntary code that helps providers and deployers of generative AI meet AI Act Art. 50(2), (4) and (5). Section 1 covers providers' machine-readable marking and detection of AI-generated or manipulated content. Section 2 covers deployers' labelling of deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest, supported by EU icons for labelling.
records.notes: Drafting began with a kick-off plenary on 5 Nov 2025. First draft 17 Dec 2025. Second draft 3 Mar 2026. Final code published 10 June 2026. On 8 July 2026 the Commission concluded that it adequately covers Art. 50(2), (4) and (5); the opinion was published 9 July 2026 and the AI Board adopted its adequacy assessment the following day. About 190 organisations had signed by end of July 2026. Adherence does not conclusively prove compliance.

verification.note: The Commission policy page confirmed the two sections, the drafting timeline (final code 10 June 2026) and about 190 signatories. The Commission news item of 10 June 2026 confirmed publication. The Commission opinion page confirmed the assessment concluded on 8 July 2026.

records.title: Action Plan on Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence
records.short_title: EU Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI
records.issuing_body: European Commission
records.summary: A Commission Communication on the risks advanced AI poses for cybersecurity, such as automated attacks and vulnerability discovery at scale. Actions include building an EU third-party evaluation capacity for advanced AI model capabilities and risks in support of the AI Office, an ENISA blueprint for structured access to advanced AI for cyber defence, and a secure testing platform with the JRC for critical sectors. It also covers stronger NIS2 and Cyber Resilience Act implementation.
records.notes: Adopted 7 July 2026 in Strasbourg. Included because its main focus is risks from advanced AI and pre-market model evaluation, which is safety content, not industrial policy. By contrast, the AI Continent Action Plan (COM(2025) 165, 9 Apr 2025) and the Apply AI Strategy (COM(2025) 723, Oct 2025) were reviewed and excluded as primarily adoption, investment and competitiveness strategies with only high-level references to trustworthy or safe AI.

verification.note: The Commission library page confirmed the title, date of 7 July 2026 and objectives. The Commission news page of 7 July 2026 confirmed the key actions (evaluation capacity, ENISA blueprint, testing platform). Council document ST-11711-2026-INIT confirmed the reference COM(2026) 577 final, dated 7 July 2026.

records.title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
records.issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
records.summary: Targeted amendment to the AI Act. It postpones high-risk obligations to fixed dates (2 Dec 2027 for Annex III, 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I) and adds a new prohibition on AI systems that generate non-consensual sexual or intimate content or child sexual abuse material. It also shortens the grace period for marking AI-generated content, strengthens AI Office supervision of AI systems built on GPAI models and of AI embedded in very large online platforms and search engines, and extends SME simplifications to small mid-caps.
records.notes: Commission proposal COM(2025) 836 of 19 Nov 2025, part of the Digital Omnibus/simplification package. As proposed, high-risk application would have been tied to the availability of standards and support tools, with a maximum delay of 16 months. Council general approach 13 Mar 2026. Provisional trilogue agreement 7 May 2026. Coreper endorsement 13 May 2026. EP plenary vote 16 Jun 2026 (423–57–174). Council final adoption 29 Jun 2026. Signed 8 Jul 2026. Published in OJ L 24 Jul 2026 (from secondary reporting, consistent with entry into force on the third day after publication). In force 27 Jul 2026. Key dates: 2 Aug 2026, general AI Act application incl. Art. 50 and AI Office powers (Arts 75, 75a–75d); 2 Dec 2026, new Art. 5 prohibition, and Art. 50(2) marking deadline for generative systems placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026 (grace period cut from 6 to 3 months); 2 Aug 2027, at least one national sandbox per Member State; 2 Dec 2027, Annex III high-risk; 2 Aug 2028, Annex I high-risk. It also reinstates (simplified) EU-database registration for systems claimed exempt under Art. 6(3), and allows processing of special-category data for bias detection only where strictly necessary. The AI Office's supervision of GPAI-based systems excludes uses such as law enforcement, border management, judicial authorities and financial institutions. Machinery is exempted from direct applicability, with delegated acts for health and safety requirements. Also amends Regulations (EU) 2018/1139 (aviation safety) and (EU) 2023/1230 (machinery). The separate horizontal Digital Omnibus (data/GDPR) is not AI-specific and is not recorded here.

verification.note: EUR-Lex ELI page loaded and confirmed the title, act date of 8 July 2026, and first entry-into-force date of 27 July 2026 (metadata). Council press releases of 7 May 2026 (agreement) and 29 June 2026 (final adoption) confirmed the content and dates. The Commission news item 'AI Omnibus enters into force' (27 July 2026) confirmed the 2 Dec 2027 and 2 Aug 2028 dates. The EP Legislative Train confirmed COM(2025) 836, 19 Nov 2025, 2025/0359(COD) and the plenary vote of 16 June 2026.

records.title: Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the 'AI Act')
records.issuing_body: European Commission
records.summary: Non-binding Commission guidelines on the Art. 50 duties, which apply from 2 Aug 2026. They cover disclosure that a user is interacting with an AI system, machine-readable marking and detectability of AI-generated or manipulated content, notice of emotion recognition and biometric categorisation, labelling of deepfakes and AI-generated public-interest text, and horizontal accessibility requirements.
records.notes: Draft guidelines were published for consultation on 8 May 2026. The final guidelines were annexed to a Commission Communication approving their content, C(2026) 5054 final of 20 July 2026. They complement the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content. Under the Digital Omnibus, generative systems placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026 have until 2 Dec 2026 to meet Art. 50(2) marking.

verification.note: The Commission news page confirmed publication on 20 July 2026 and the content. The official PDF on the AI Act Service Desk confirmed the exact title and the C(2026) 5054 final reference dated 20.7.2026.

records.issuing_body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources – National Artificial Intelligence Centre
records.summary: Australia's current voluntary AI governance guidance for industry. It sets out six essential practices for responsible AI governance and adoption, based on Australia's AI Ethics Principles and international standards. records.title: National AI Plan
records.issuing_body: Australian Government (Department of Industry, Science and Resources)
records.summary: Australia's flagship AI policy, built on three goals with three pillars each. On safety, it takes a practical, risk-based approach that relies on existing technology-neutral laws and regulators instead of mandatory AI-specific guardrails or a standalone AI Act. It funds an Australian AI Safety Institute to monitor and test frontier AI and advise government.
records.notes: Released on 2 Dec 2025, according to the Government's 1 Apr 2026 response to the Senate Select Committee on Adopting AI. That decision replaced the earlier plan for mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI. Related measures cited in the response: a committed but not yet legislated Digital Duty of Care; a planned legislative framework for automated decision-making in government; Privacy Act disclosure of substantially automated decisions from 10 Dec 2026 (Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024); and the 2024 deepfake sexual material offences. Later DISR MoUs with Anthropic (1 Apr 2026) and Microsoft (23 Apr 2026) cite the Plan.

verification.note: The Plan's own DISR page could not be located: guessed URLs returned 404 and the web search budget was exhausted. The 2 Dec 2025 release date, three-goal structure and reliance on existing laws were confirmed from the official Government response to the Senate Select Committee (industry.gov.au, 1 Apr 2026). records.title: Australian AI Safety Institute (establishment)
records.issuing_body: Australian Government (Department of Industry, Science and Resources)
records.summary: Sets up an Australian AI Safety Institute to monitor, test and share information about emerging AI capabilities and risks. It will advise ministers, agencies and regulators, test frontier AI models, act as a hub for coordinated government action and support Australia's international AI safety commitments. It is explicitly not a regulator and complements existing laws.
records.notes: Funding: A$29.8 million over four years from 2025-26, then A$7.9 million a year ongoing from 2029-30 (per the Senate committee response). The DISR news page is dated 25 November 2025 and states that the minister announced the Australian AI Safety Institute on that day, shortly before the National AI Plan; the page also carries an 'Updated 17 December' note on the renaming of the International Network of AI Safety Institutes to the 'International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science'. A DISR MoU with Canada on AI safety institute collaboration was published on 5 Mar 2026.

verification.note: DISR news page fetched: mandate, non-regulatory role and network membership confirmed; the page is dated 25 November 2025 (confirmed on the stored copy in the 11 Oct 2026 quality check). records.title: Superior Electoral Court Resolution No. 23,732 of 27 February 2024 (amending Resolution 23,610/2019 on electoral propaganda: AI and synthetic content rules)

records.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making
records.issuing_body: Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat
records.summary: Mandatory Treasury Board policy instrument requiring federal institutions that use automated decision systems for administrative decisions to complete an Algorithmic Impact Assessment and apply risk-tiered safeguards: notice and explanation, peer review, testing and monitoring for bias and quality, human intervention for higher-impact decisions, and recourse.
records.notes: Binding on federal institutions as Treasury Board policy (not a statute). Launched 4 March 2019; effective April 2019, with compliance required for new systems from 1 April 2020. Amended 1 April 2021, 25 April 2023 (third review) and 24 June 2025 (fourth review: more transparency, stronger testing/monitoring and senior-level accountability; Algorithmic Impact Assessment updated). Reviewed every two years.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Part 3 of Bill C-27, Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022)
records.issuing_body: Parliament of Canada (Government bill sponsored by the Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry)
records.summary: Would have created Canada's first federal AI statute, imposing risk-based obligations on 'high-impact' AI systems (risk assessment and mitigation, monitoring, record-keeping, transparency, notification of material harm), an AI and Data Commissioner, and offences for deploying AI that causes serious harm. It never passed committee stage and died when Parliament was prorogued.
records.notes: Introduced 16 June 2022 (first reading); referred to the Standing Committee on Industry and Technology 24 April 2023; last committee meeting 26 Sept 2024; died on the Order Paper when the 1st Session of the 44th Parliament was prorogued on 6 Jan 2025. No AIDA successor as of Oct 2026: the June 2026 National AI Strategy relies on privacy and online-safety law modernisation instead. Bill C-36 (Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, first reading 15 June 2026, sponsored by the Minister of AI and Digital Innovation) re-enacts only the privacy part of C-27 (incl. automated-decision-system disclosure) and is excluded here as a general privacy law. AI Minister Evan Solomon said in late Sept 2026 that AI deployment needs regulation but gave no details (press report, not an official source).

verification.note: LEGISinfo page confirms full title, first reading 16 June 2022, last stage 'consideration in committee' (not completed) and session end 6 Jan 2025. ISED AIDA page loads as an archived page (modified 2025-12-09). Bill C-36 details confirmed on LEGISinfo 45-1/c-36.

records.issuing_body: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)

records.summary: Government-wide strategy for responsible AI adoption in federal institutions: lifecycle governance and risk frameworks proportionate to impact, ethics review of higher-risk projects with controls including emergency shutdown, security and reliability controls, an AI Centre of Expertise, and public transparency through a Government of Canada AI Register.

records.title: Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All
records.short_title: Canada National AI Strategy (AI for All)
records.issuing_body: Government of Canada – Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation / Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
records.summary: Refreshed flagship national AI strategy built on opportunity, trust and sovereignty. Its trust pillar commits to modernising privacy and online-safety laws, legal tools against deepfakes and for safe chatbot interactions, AI transparency work (including watermarking) and a Canada Trusted AI Certification program, renewal of the Standards Council's AI program, CAD 50M to expand the Canadian AI Safety Institute, and work with frontier AI companies and partners against cyber and national-security threats from advanced AI.
records.notes: Announced by PM Mark Carney 4 June 2026 (ISED news release 5 June 2026; page created 3 June, modified 8 June 2026). Successor to the Pan-Canadian AI Strategy (2017). Does not propose a stand-alone AI statute to replace AIDA. Follow-on measures: Bill C-34 (Safe Social Media Act, 10 June 2026) and Bill C-36 (privacy reform, 15 June 2026). An ISED consultation 'Advancing AI transparency in Canada' reportedly ran 23 July–23 Sept 2026 (per press; the ISED page could not be fetched). Built on a national consultation (11,000+ submissions) and a 28-member AI Strategy Task Force.

records.title: Bill regulating artificial intelligence systems (Bulletins 16821-19 and 15869-19, merged)
records.original_title: Proyecto de ley que regula los sistemas de inteligencia artificial (Boletín N° 16821-19, refundido con Boletín N° 15869-19)
records.issuing_body: National Congress of Chile (Executive bill; passed Chamber of Deputies, now in the Senate)
records.summary: EU-style risk-based AI bill: unacceptable-risk systems (e.g., subliminal manipulation, categorisation using sensitive data, indiscriminate facial recognition) are banned; high-risk systems need risk management, technical documentation, human oversight, cybersecurity and post-deployment monitoring; limited-risk systems carry transparency duties; includes incident reporting.
records.notes: Executive bill submitted in May 2024 (exact date not re-verified) and merged with motion 15869-19. Chamber of Deputies approved it in general 4 Aug 2025 (63-47-6) and dispatched it 13 Oct 2025 to the second constitutional stage (Senate); articles on an advisory council, enforcement by the Personal Data Protection Agency and regulatory sandboxes were rejected. In the Senate's Future Challenges Committee: general study still ongoing at the 13 July 2026 session (simple urgency). On 26 May 2026 the new government's Science Minister Ximena Lincolao presented a lighter, innovation-focused framework (ex post rather than ex ante review) that senators expect to be filed as a substitute amendment. Final content therefore uncertain.

records.title: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendation for Internet Information Services
records.original_title: 互联网信息服务算法推荐管理规定
records.issuing_body: Cyberspace Administration of China; Ministry of Industry and Information Technology; Ministry of Public Security; State Administration for Market Regulation
records.summary: China's first binding AI-specific rule (35 articles). It covers algorithmic recommendation services, including generation/synthesis, personalised push, ranking, search filtering and scheduling/decision-making. It requires algorithm security management and assessment, transparency about how the algorithm works, a user option to switch off personalised recommendation, conspicuous labelling of algorithmically generated or synthetic content, and protections for minors, the elderly, workers and consumers. It also created the CAC algorithm filing (registry) system for providers with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity.
records.notes: Adopted at the CAC office meeting of 16 Nov 2021, signed 31 Dec 2021, published on cac.gov.cn 4 Jan 2022 and in State Council Gazette 2022 No. 9. Still in force as of Oct 2026, with no amendment found. The algorithm filing system it created also serves the deep synthesis, generative AI and anthropomorphic AI rules.

records.title: Interim Measures for the Administration of Anthropomorphic AI Interaction Services
records.original_title: 人工智能拟人化互动服务管理暂行办法
records.issuing_body: Cyberspace Administration of China; National Development and Reform Commission; Ministry of Industry and Information Technology; Ministry of Public Security; State Administration for Market Regulation
records.summary: Regulates AI services that simulate human personality and give ongoing emotional companionship (32 articles). It bans virtual partner or relative services for minors, requires guardian consent for under-14s and a minor mode, and requires clear disclosure that the user is talking to AI. Other duties include reminders after every 2 hours of continuous use, measures against emotional dependence, crisis intervention for self-harm risk, easy exit, and limits on using sensitive chat data for training. Security assessments are required at launch, after major changes, and at 1 million registered or 100,000 monthly active users, and algorithms must be filed.
records.notes: The draft for comment was released 27 Dec 2025. Adopted at the CAC office meeting of 2 Feb 2026, promulgated 10 Apr 2026, effective 15 Jul 2026, and published in the 2026 State Council Gazette No. 17. Penalties range from warnings to service suspension and fines of RMB 10,000–100,000, or RMB 100,000–200,000 where harm to life or health occurs. It also calls for an AI sandbox safety service platform. Task-oriented tools without ongoing emotional interaction, such as customer service bots, are excluded.

records.title: Act on supplementary provisions to the Regulation on Artificial Intelligence
records.original_title: Lov om supplerende bestemmelser til forordningen om kunstig intelligens
records.issuing_body: Folketing (Ministry of Digital Affairs / Forsknings-, Uddannelses- og Digitaliseringsministeriet)
records.summary: Denmark's law implementing the enforcement framework of the EU AI Act. It names the Agency for Digital Government (Digitaliseringsstyrelsen) as national competent authority, notifying authority, single point of contact and market surveillance authority for some prohibited practices. The Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet) and the Danish Courts Administration supervise specific areas. Authorities get powers to request information, inspect premises and order or ban risky AI systems, and fines apply for breaches of the prohibitions.
records.notes: Bill L 154 (2024-25 session) was introduced on 26 Feb 2025 by Minister for Digital Affairs Caroline Stage Olsen. records.title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026
records.short_title: IT Rules amendment on synthetically generated information (deepfake labelling), 2026
records.issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India
records.official_identifier: G.S.R. 120(E), dated 10 February 2026 (amending the IT Rules 2021, G.S.R. 139(E))
records.summary: Binding amendment to India's intermediary rules for AI-generated content. It defines 'synthetically generated information' (SGI). Platforms that offer SGI-creation tools must technically prevent unlawful SGI (e.g. CSAM, non-consensual intimate imagery, deceptive depictions of real people or events). Other SGI must carry a prominent label and, where feasible, permanent metadata or a provenance identifier, and platforms must not let users remove either. Significant social media intermediaries must collect user declarations on whether content is SGI, verify them technically and label confirmed SGI. The rules also cut takedown deadlines to 3 hours (from 36), and to 2 hours for intimate or morphed imagery complaints.

The final rules were notified on 10 Feb 2026 and took effect on 20 Feb 2026, according to multiple law-firm trackers (e.g. S.S. Rana, AZB). The rules follow MeitY's non-binding AI advisories to intermediaries of 1 Mar 2024 (revised 15 Mar 2024, which dropped a prior-approval requirement for 'under-tested' models). Those advisories are not separately recorded because no primary copy could be fetched. A further draft 'Second Amendment' to the IT Rules was published on 30 Mar 2026 (revised 21 Apr 2026; comments closed 7 May 2026). High-impact AI operators must confirm high-impact status, adopt risk management, explainability, user protection and human oversight measures, and should conduct fundamental-rights impact assessments (Arts. 33–35). Promulgated 21 Jan 2025 and in force one year later, on 22 Jan 2026 (Addenda Art. 1); the digital medical device part of Art. 2(4)(d) applies from 24 Jan 2026. Enforcement powers include fact-finding investigations and stop or correction orders (Art. 40). Administrative fines of up to KRW 30 million apply for failing to give AI notice, failing to appoint a domestic agent, or ignoring orders (Art. 43). Details such as the compute threshold and high-impact criteria are set by Presidential Enforcement Decree.

records.title: Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (Executive Order 14365)
records.issuing_body: The White House (President Donald J. Trump)
records.summary: Seeks a 'minimally burdensome' national AI standard and targets state AI laws. It creates a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state laws and has Commerce identify 'onerous' state AI laws. It conditions BEAD non-deployment funds and other discretionary grants on state AI policy, directs an FCC proceeding on a preemptive federal reporting and disclosure standard, and requires an FTC policy statement on when state laws that force changes to truthful AI outputs are preempted. It also calls for preemptive federal legislation that spares state child-safety, AI infrastructure and state-procurement laws.
records.notes: Signed 11 Dec 2025; published 16 Dec 2025. Implementation: (1) The AG memo of 9 Jan 2026 established the AI Litigation Task Force. (2) The Commerce evaluation, BEAD policy notice, FTC statement and FCC proceeding were due about 11 Mar 2026. Secondary sources reported in April 2026 that the Commerce list had not been made public; no later publication could be verified. (3) The White House released its legislative recommendations on 20 Mar 2026. (4) On 24 Apr 2026 DOJ filed a companion complaint in xAI's federal suit against Colorado SB 24-205 (D. Colo.); Colorado's AG agreed to a stipulated order pausing enforcement (27 Apr 2026), and Colorado repealed and replaced the law in May 2026. (5) The FTC issued a Proposed Policy Statement on 1 Jul 2026. No federal preemption statute had been enacted as of Oct 2026. An earlier 10-year state-AI-law moratorium in the 2025 reconciliation bill was removed by a 99-1 Senate vote in July 2025, and preemption bills (e.g. H.R. 5388, American Artificial Intelligence Leadership and Uniformity Act, introduced 16 Sep 2025; the FRONTIER Act, July 2026) remain pending. No court ruling on the EO itself was identified.

records.title: Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security (Executive Order 14409)
records.issuing_body: The White House (President Donald J. Trump)

records.title: Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act (FRONTIER Act)
records.issuing_body: U.S. House of Representatives (Reps. Jay Obernolte, Lori Trahan, Scott Franklin, Scott Peters, Erin Houchin, Suhas Subramanyam)
records.summary: Bipartisan federal frontier-AI bill covering models trained on more than 10^26 operations. Large and very large developers (tiered by revenue and AI R&D spend) would publish frontier AI frameworks, register, undergo annual independent audits, report critical safety incidents, and for the largest tier retain a licensed independent verification organisation. A new Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security would administer it. The Commerce Secretary would gain emergency power to suspend models posing imminent catastrophic risk, and new state obligations on catastrophic-risk transparency, auditing and incident reporting would be preempted.
records.notes: Introduced 23 Jul 2026; the House bill number could not be confirmed (congress.gov blocked). The section-by-section says preemption targets state frontier-safety laws such as CA SB 53, NY RAISE and 'IL SB-315', while saving generally applicable, deployment-based, child-protection and procurement laws. Penalties up to $1M per violation per day, and $10M per day for emergency-order violations. On 4 Jun 2026 the same lead sponsors released the broader 'Great American AI Act' discussion draft (a three-year freeze on state AI development rules, CAISI codification); per secondary sources it had not been formally introduced as of Sep 2026. On 1 Oct 2026 the sponsors welcomed the White House Accord and urged that it be codified through this bill. No committee action verified.

records.title: Act on Market Surveillance and the Promotion of Innovation in Artificial Intelligence (KI-MIG)
records.original_title: Gesetz zur Marktüberwachung und Innovationsförderung von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI-Marktüberwachungs-und-Innovationsförderungs-Gesetz – KI-MIG)
records.issuing_body: Federal Republic of Germany: Bundestag with the consent of the Bundesrat (promulgated in the Bundesgesetzblatt)
records.summary: Germany's national implementing law for the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). It makes the Bundesnetzagentur the central market surveillance authority, single point of contact and complaints body, with sector regulators such as BaFin keeping their remits; creates an AI market surveillance chamber and a coordination and competence centre; defines the authorities' powers; provides for AI regulatory sandboxes (KI-Reallabore) and real-world testing of high-risk systems outside sandboxes; and lays down fines, record-keeping duties, an evaluation clause and a register of certain high-risk AI systems.
records.notes: Dated 22 July 2026 and promulgated in Bundesgesetzblatt 2026 I No. 223; in force from 29 July 2026 under Article 5, a few days before the AI Act's main obligations applied on 2 August 2026. Structure: Part 1 scope; Part 2 competent authorities and cooperation (§§ 2-10, incl. the KI-Marktüberwachungskammer, the coordination and competence centre, the central contact point and complaints office); Part 3 powers (§ 11); Part 4 innovation support (§§ 12-14, KI-Reallabore and real-world testing of high-risk systems); Part 5 fines (§§ 15-17); Part 6 retention duties; Part 7 evaluation; Part 8 register of certain high-risk AI systems (§ 20). Press reports give the cabinet draft as 11 Feb 2026, Bundestag passage as 11 June 2026 and Bundesrat approval in July 2026.

verification.note: gesetze-im-internet.de (Federal Ministry of Justice portal) fetched: law header and table of contents. Full title, abbreviation KI-MIG, Ausfertigungsdatum 22.07.2026, Fundstelle BGBl. 2026 I Nr. 223, entry into force 29.07.2026 (Art. 5), § 2(1) naming the Bundesnetzagentur as the market surveillance authority, and the section structure (§§ 1-20) confirmed. records.title: Law on Artificial Intelligence
records.original_title: Luật Trí tuệ nhân tạo
records.short_title: Viet Nam Law on Artificial Intelligence (2025)
records.issuing_body: National Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam (15th National Assembly, 10th session)
records.summary: Viet Nam's first dedicated AI law, passed on 10 December 2025 by 429 of 434 deputies present and in force from 1 March 2026. In 8 chapters and 35 articles it governs the research, development, provision, deployment and use of AI systems and the state management of AI; classifies systems as high, medium or low risk, with management measures proportionate to the risk; encourages controlled testing of technology and voluntary compliance mechanisms; prioritises AI in public administration and public services; treats data, computing and safe AI infrastructure as strategic national assets; and excludes AI used solely for national defence, security or cipher purposes.
records.notes: High risk is defined as possible significant harm to life, health, rights, national security or the public interest; medium risk as possible confusion or manipulation of users who do not realise they are interacting with AI or AI-generated content. Legal databases (not official pages) give the law number 134/2025/QH15, Official Gazette No. 40-01/2026 of 22 Jan 2026, Article 7 prohibited acts, mandatory labelling of AI-generated content, transition periods of 12 to 18 months for existing systems depending on sector, and a Prime Minister's implementation plan (Decision 367/QĐ-TTg of 4 Mar 2026). The official_url is the National Assembly's newspaper report of the vote.

records.title: REAIM Blueprint for Action
records.issuing_body: Participating states of the REAIM Summit 2024, co-organised by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of National Defense of the Republic of Korea; supported by 61 states
records.summary: Outcome document of the second Responsible AI in the Military Domain (REAIM) summit, held in Seoul on 9-10 September 2024 and endorsed at its closing session by 61 states. The declarative, non-binding Blueprint sets out a roadmap and principles for the governance of AI in the military domain: compliance with international law, human responsibility and accountability, reliable and trustworthy AI, appropriate human involvement, and improved explainability. It builds on the 2023 REAIM Call to Action from The Hague.
records.notes: The official_url is the host ministry's press release on the summit outcome (dated 10 Sep 2024), which confirms the endorsement and the headline principles. Press reports state that China attended but did not endorse the document (not confirmed on an official page). Later REAIM outcomes are not yet in the register.

records.title: The UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
records.issuing_body: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications Office (UAE AI Office)
records.summary: Charter of twelve principles for the development and use of AI in the UAE: a beneficial human-machine relationship; safety, with risky systems to be modified or removed; fairness and the avoidance of algorithmic bias; data privacy; transparency; human oversight; governance and accountability; technological excellence; commitment to human values; peaceful coexistence; inclusive AI awareness; and compliance with treaties and applicable law. It is a statement of principles aligned with the UAE AI Strategy 2031, not legislation.
records.notes: The charter PDF on ai.gov.ae is in a folder dated July 2024 and press reports give the launch as late July 2024; the UAE legislation portal reportedly lists 10 June 2024 as the issue date, so date_published is given as 2024-07 only. The issuing body is taken from press reports; the u.ae page does not name it. ai.gov.ae and uaelegislation.gov.ae return HTTP 403 to automated requests, so the archiver may only store the u.ae page.

records.title: AI Ethics Principles
records.issuing_body: Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA)
records.summary: Saudi Arabia's national AI ethics framework, issued by SDAIA to support the Kingdom's AI strategies, govern data and AI models so as to limit the negative effects of AI systems, and help entities adopt ethics standards when building AI solutions. It sets out seven principles (fairness, privacy and security, humanity, social and environmental benefits, reliability and safety, transparency and explainability, and accountability and responsibility) with associated controls across the AI system life cycle, including continuous monitoring, performance reporting, predefined triggers and human oversight in the deploy-and-monitor stage, and assigns roles and responsibilities, with SDAIA developing and updating the principles, preparing national guides and standards, and monitoring compliance.
records.notes: The PDF at the official URL carries the year 2025 on its cover and 'Version Number 1' in its document-control table; no month is given, so date_published is 2025. Law-firm commentaries describe an earlier version 2.0 of September 2023 (which introduced risk tiers from low to unacceptable) and a version 1.0 of 2022; the 2025 edition does not state how it relates to that numbering. Commentators disagree on whether the principles are binding on the entities in scope; the document itself describes SDAIA as monitoring compliance, so it is recorded here as non-binding guidance pending clarification. SDAIA's generative AI guidelines and the draft Global AI Hub Law are not yet in the register.
